newsitem.title: USA: Airport anti-terror measures clear U.S. House.
newsitem.headline: Airport anti-terror measures clear U.S. House.

text.p: The House of Representatives approved a wide-ranging aviation bill on Friday that steps up airport security against terrorist attacks.

The bill also established rules for record-setting flights stemming from the crash of a plane this year in which 7-year-old Jessica Dubroff was killed while trying to become the youngest pilot to fly across the country.
The rules would bar anyone without a valid pilot's certificate and medical certificate from handling the controls of a plane while trying to set a record.

Among the anti-terorrism provisions were requirements that airlines do background checks on employees screening passengers, baggage and cargo and that the Federal Aviation Administration certify security firms doing the screening.

Also in the measure were reforms of the way airlines deal with families of crash victims. They were taken from a separate bill drafted after complaints by families of victims of the July 17 TWA 800 crash off Long Island, New York.

Most of the debate on the bill concerned a provision reclassifying employees of Federal Express as covered by the Railway Labor Act rather than the National Labor Relations Act. The change, which would require employees to organize nationally rather than being allowed to organize locally, would make it more difficult for them to strike.
Its proponents said the change was merely correcting a technical error in earlier legislation. Opponents called it a payoff for special interests.
The bill, which provided $19 billion for the Federal Aviation Administration for two years, was sent to the Senate.
